summary:
Gorontalo stands under Indonesia's national framework: the revised penal code, the national security posture and the policing practice described below apply in the province, and the source inventory records no ordinance, raid, protection measure or support service specific to Gorontalo in either direction.

Indonesia does not expressly criminalise consensual same-sex activity between adults in private, but the penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and punishes consensual extra-marital sex with imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision effectively reaches consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The custodial maximum is given as two years in one source and one year in another. Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protection and no hate-crime protection for LGBT people.

Legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery followed by judicial approval. There is no administrative route to a changed marker that avoids surgery and a court order.

Morality enforcement is sharpest in Aceh, where Sharia applies and homosexuality is punishable by flogging or imprisonment; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and Aceh's penalties reach anyone present in the province, foreign visitors included. Other provinces carry morality provisions of the same family.

Violence risk is documented at the level of state action and at the level of mobs. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena stated the gathering violated no law. Vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia in a wave on 14-16 July 2026, most severely in Bogor where more than fifteen trans women were doused, stripped and beaten and footage was circulated online. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a trans Peruvian Harvard student, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges in 2022 while on honeymoon in Bali and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him and Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a threat. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to the July 2026 mob attacks. Researchers record markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016, and a 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians rate homosexuality morally unacceptable. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Aceh is the outlier rather than the national norm: its Sharia punishments, including the caning of two men in February 2025, are harsher than anything documented elsewhere in Indonesia, and they apply to visitors who travel there. A trans visitor who never enters Aceh is not exposed to that specific penalty regime but remains covered by the national penal code and by provincial morality laws of the same family elsewhere.

Enforcement is not confined to Aceh. The Puncak villa raid of 22 June 2025 and the mob attacks of 14-16 July 2026 both occurred outside the special religious-law province, which indicates that police deployment and vigilante violence are available across the country rather than concentrated in one jurisdiction.

The societal climate is measured directly. A researcher cited in The Diplomat records markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016, and the 2025 Pew figure of 93% rating homosexuality morally unacceptable gives the scale of that shift. The October 2025 presidential decree places the same hostility inside national defence doctrine, so the risk a visitor encounters is not only criminal law but an official framing of LGBTQ+ people as a security matter.

Documentary procedure is a practical obstacle independent of street risk: sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval is the only route to a changed gender marker, which affects how a trans visitor's passport or other documents read at immigration and hotel registration.
localsOnly:
Indonesians live under the same penal code that took effect on 2 January 2026, which punishes consensual extra-marital sex and, given the absence of same-sex marriage, effectively reaches consensual same-sex relations. Reporting describes prosecutions as selective rather than systematic.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate-crime law enhances penalties for violence committed against them. Attacks such as those of 14-16 July 2026 therefore proceed without an aggravating offence attached to their anti-LGBTQ+ character.

Changing a gender marker on Indonesian identity documents requires sex-reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. Indonesians who cannot meet both conditions continue to present documents that do not match their lived gender.

Provincial morality provisions and, in Aceh, Sharia penalties including flogging are imposed on residents as well as on visitors. Residents of Gorontalo are subject to the national framework, and nothing in the audited material records a provincial protection mechanism, a designated service or an official outreach programme for them.
outOfScopeNotes:
The custodial maximum for the extra-marital sex offence is recorded inconsistently across the sources: two years in the national country profile and one year in the encyclopedia account of the 2022 amendment. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory addresses Gorontalo directly. The encyclopedia page for Gorontalo yielded no usable finding, so whether the province has its own morality bylaw, a raid history or a documented protection measure is not sourced either way; the dossier states the absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

Outcomes are unresolved: no source records whether the perpetrators of the 14-16 July 2026 attacks were investigated or charged, whether the 75 people arrested at Puncak on 22 June 2025 were prosecuted, or whether the circumstances of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla's death in 2022 were reviewed.

The frequency of enforcement in practice is not quantified in the inventory; only the cited incidents and the description of prosecutions as selective bear on it.
